name: Coulter
note: A coulter is a sharp disc mounted at the front of a plough that cuts through soil and plants vertically before the plough blade reaches it. It is not the plough itself but a separate cutting tool that runs just ahead, slicing through roots and compacted earth to make the plough's work easier and cleaner.

name: Ridging plough
note: A ridging plough has a mouldboard on each side of a central share, so it throws soil both ways and builds a raised ridge with a furrow between. The ridges drain excess water, which helps root crops that rot if waterlogged, and they warm faster in spring. It needs strong draught animals, which the horse collar provides.

name: Subsoiler
note: A subsoiler is a narrow, strong tine that runs deep, below normal ploughing depth, to break up hardpan, a compacted layer that stops roots and water going down. Unlike a plough with a mouldboard, it shatters the deep layer in place without turning the soil over. It needs a lot of pulling power, hence the horse collar.

name: Harrow
note: A harrow is a frame set with teeth (tines) that is dragged across a ploughed field. It breaks up clods, levels the surface, covers scattered seed and pulls out weeds. It needs a draught animal strong enough to pull it, and tines of wood or iron. The spacing and angle of the tines matter most on heavy clay, where clods are hard and the tines can clog or skip over them.

name: Roller
note: A heavy cylinder drawn across a ploughed field to break clods and press the soil firm around seed. Its weight and its bearings decide how much clod-breaking it achieves without crushing the soil into a crust. It needs a horse collar so that horses can pull the load, a stone or iron cylinder and a frame. Too light and it does nothing; too heavy and it packs wet soil hard.

name: Cultivator
note: A horse-drawn frame with tines (curved iron teeth) that loosen and weed the soil between crop rows. An adjustable parallelogram linkage keeps the tines parallel and the depth constant even as the ground rises and falls. It needs a rigid horse collar for pulling and iron parts. Without the linkage the tines dive into the soil or skip over it, and damage the crop.

name: Horse hoe
note: Simple cultivator or hoe frame pulled by horse along seed drill rows to cut weeds between plants. Requires plants spaced precisely by the drill. Eliminates hand-hoeing drudgery and allows larger plantings.

name: Seed drill
kb: A mechanical hopper with toothed wheels dropping seed at precise intervals into furrows opened by running tines.
note: Not just broadcasting but timed metering per revolution, spacing seed 4-6 inches in straight rows at depth

name: Reaper
note: The eccentric cam driving the sickle bar at the right frequency and the gathering platform timing, not just a rotating blade

name: Reaper-binder
note: A reaper cuts standing grain; a binder also gathers the cut stalks into bundles (sheaves) and ties each with twine, so no one has to follow the machine tying by hand. The hard part is the knotter, a mechanism of small moving hooks and a knife that must form a reliable knot round each sheaf at working speed. It needs a working reaper and precise metal parts, and it saves the large labour of binding at harvest, when time is short.

name: Combine harvester
note: Reaper feeds cut grain into threshing drum and winnowing mechanism; discharges bagged grain and straw bales. Steam- or petrol-powered. Requires flat or gentle ground, good visibility, and skilled operators. 20-30 acres per day vs 1 acre hand harvest.

name: Mower
note: A horse-drawn machine that cuts grass for hay. Its cutter bar moves a sickle (a row of triangular blades) to and fro through fixed guards, a scissor action copied from grain reaping but adapted for the softer stems and lower height of grass. It needs the reaper and a horse collar. Blades must be kept sharp, and the cutter bar clogs in wet or lodged (flattened) grass.

name: Tedder
note: A horse-drawn machine that tosses cut hay into the air so it dries evenly in the sun and wind. The tines must turn at the right speed relative to the forward motion, so hay is thrown upward and backward and spread evenly. It needs a horse collar and an iron frame. Poor timing leaves hay in clumps that rot in the stack.

name: Baler
note: A machine that compresses hay or straw into dense bales and ties them. A double-screw compression mechanism packs the bale densely and a knotter ties twine around it as the machine moves. It needs steam power and high pressure boilers, and well-made gears and twine. It saves storage space and eases transport, but a bale that is too moist heats and may catch fire.

name: Threshing machine
note: Flailed drum rotating against fixed comb beats grain from heads mechanically, replacing hand flailing. Powered by horses treading or pulled by oxen. Three to five fold increase in threshing speed. Multiplies bottleneck from threshing to grinding.

name: Winnower
note: Winnowing separates grain from chaff, the light husk and dust left after threshing. The mixture is dropped through a stream of air, so the lighter chaff is blown aside while the heavier grain falls nearly straight down. A winnowing machine replaces waiting for the wind with a hand-turned fan. The airflow has to be set right: too weak leaves chaff in the grain, too strong blows good grain away.

name: Fanning mill
note: The combination of vibrating screens, fan speed modulation, and multiple air streams that grade by size and weight in one pass

name: Root cutter
note: A hand or horse-powered machine that slices turnips, mangolds and other roots into chips for feeding livestock. Blades set at the right angle and spacing produce small chips without clogging or needing hand-feeding. It needs a horse collar for powered use and iron blades. Large chunks can choke an animal, so chip size matters.

name: Chaff cutter
note: A machine that chops straw or hay into short lengths (chaff) for animal feed. Rotating blades slice the straw as it is fed past them. It is simple, but the blade speed and feed rate determine how consistent the length is and how safe it is for the operator's hands. It needs iron blades and a frame. Poorly chopped straw is wasted and animals sort it out.

name: Potato lifter
note: A horse-drawn plough-like machine that digs up potatoes from the ridges and shakes the soil off. The tine spacing and angle lift the potatoes and shake off soil without burying them again or cutting them. It needs a horse collar and a ridging plough, which makes the ridges they grow in. Bruised or cut tubers rot in storage.

name: Steam tractor
note: A steam engine mounted on wheels that pulls ploughs and machinery in the field. The efficiency of the compound cylinder (steam used in two stages) saves fuel, and the differential gear lets the rear wheels turn at different speeds on curves. It needs a high pressure boiler, water and coal. It is heavy and expensive, and sinks into soft ground.

name: Caterpillar track
kb: An endless track of linked plates replacing wheels to distribute weight and prevent sinking in soft ground.
note: The idler and tensioner that keep tracks tight over soft mud, and the steering clutch for each side

name: Power take-off shaft
note: The universal joint coupling that lets the shaft angle without binding, the clutch that disengages without stopping the engine

name: Three-point linkage
note: A hitch in which an implement is attached to the tractor at three points, so the weight transfers to the tractor's rear wheels and improves grip. The lower links adjust the depth automatically according to soil resistance, freeing the driver to steer. It needs a steam tractor and a power take-off shaft. Its design needs careful geometry; a poor set keeps the implement from holding a depth.

name: Liming
note: Spreading lime on acid soil to neutralise it. In acid soil clay binds up phosphorus, and lime releases it for crops. The farmer must work out the dose for each acre and the depth of ploughing. It needs a supply of quicklime or ground limestone and a plough. Too much lime locks up other nutrients, and lime scatters poorly in wind or rain.

name: Marling
note: Marl is a crumbly natural mixture of clay and lime (calcium carbonate), dug from pits and spread on fields. The lime reduces soil acidity and the clay binds loose sandy soil, so one material corrects more than one fault. It needs a marl bed near the field, since digging and carting are heavy work, and some skill in judging which fields lack lime and which lack clay.

name: Green manure
note: Growing a crop, such as clover, and ploughing it into the soil before harvest to add nitrogen and organic matter. The timing is critical: it must be ploughed in before the seed matures, when the crop holds the most nitrogen, but not so late that decay makes the nitrogen unavailable to plants. It needs legume rotation (rotating crops that include legumes), a heavy plough and marling (spreading clay-rich lime earth).

name: Composting
note: Piling manure, straw and waste plants so they rot down into crumbly fertiliser. Controlling the temperature and moisture of the heap turns putrefaction (smelly decay) into complete decomposition in months, not years, and the heat kills weed seeds. It needs a mix of green and dry material and regular turning. A heap that is too wet turns sour, and one too dry stops.

name: The nitrogen cycle as knowledge
note: Understanding how plants obtain nitrogen. Nitrogen already in manure differs from nitrogen fixed from the air, which explains why growing legumes restores soil. Knowing the cycle lets a farmer plan rotations and fertiliser. It needs the habit of controlled experiments, with hypotheses, replication and publication. Without it, a farmer follows habits without understanding.

name: Rhizobia and legume nodulation
note: The discovery that nodules on the roots of legumes (peas, beans, clover) contain bacteria called rhizobia, which turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants can use. Nodules appear only on legumes. It needs knowledge of the nitrogen cycle and a good microscope to see the bacteria. It explains why legumes enrich the soil, and why seed is sometimes inoculated.

name: Norfolk four-course rotation
note: The insight that turnips fed to stalled cattle in winter meant no fallow was needed, so four crops per four years beats three

name: Bone meal
note: Fertiliser made by steaming and finely grinding bones. The steaming removes the fat and the fine grinding makes the phosphorus (a nutrient needed for roots and seeds) available to plants within a few years, instead of decades for raw bones. It needs a supply of bones and large amounts of charcoal-scale fuel. Whole bones release phosphorus very slowly.

name: Superphosphate
kb: Bones treated with sulfuric acid to convert insoluble calcium phosphate to soluble monocalcium phosphate.
note: The acid digestion that solubilises phosphorus years ahead of bone meal, yielding 15-20% phosphate instead of 3%

name: Basic slag
note: A fertiliser made from the waste slag of steel made in a converter lined to remove phosphorus. The slag, rich in phosphate and lime, is ground to powder and spread on the field, giving a double amendment: phosphorus for crops and lime to sweeten acid soil. It needs bulk steelmaking. It is a recycling of waste, and grinding it fine is essential.

name: Potash
note: Potassium salts used as fertiliser, needed by crops for strong stems and fruit. A trial shows a dose-response curve: modest rates boost yield, but excessive rates cause the soil to become saline (salty) and harm crops. It needs a source of potash, such as wood ash or mined salts, and field trials to find the right dose. Heavy dressing is wasted.

name: Guano
note: Seabird droppings from dry islands, rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, used as a very powerful fertiliser. It is soluble enough to leach away in rain, so it must be applied in late spring and worked into the soil, not spread months ahead. It needs a surveyed and secured deposit and shipping. Overdoses burn crops, and deposits are limited and can be exhausted.

name: Ammonium sulphate from gasworks
note: Ammonium sulphate, made from the ammonia in coal gas at gasworks, by absorbing it in sulphuric acid. It is the first synthetic nitrogen fertiliser; about a fifth of it is nitrogen, and it is soluble and available to plants within weeks. It needs coal, coking and sulphuric acid (oil of vitriol). It acidifies soil with repeated use.

name: Urea as fertiliser
note: A fertiliser made by synthesis from ammonia and carbon dioxide, a pure chemical rather than a by-product or a mined mineral. It is concentrated in nitrogen and easily stored. It needs the Haber-Bosch process (making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen under pressure) and urea synthesis. Urea left on the surface loses nitrogen as ammonia gas, so it should be worked in.

name: Soil testing
note: Measuring what a soil contains. Gravimetric nitrogen determination (weighing a product to find the amount) and acid-extraction of phosphate give farmers concrete data instead of guesswork on how much fertiliser to apply. It needs gravimetric and volumetric analysis and a laboratory. A soil sample must represent the whole field, or the result misleads.

name: Tile drainage
note: Draining wet fields with buried pipes of fired clay tile. A main pipe collects water from lateral pipes laid in a pattern across the field, with the gradient calculated so water flows without silting. A filter cloth around joints stops silt from blocking them. It needs clay tiles, a plough or trench digger and a horse collar. Poor gradients clog, and the work is hidden once buried.

name: Gravity and pump irrigation
note: Watering fields through channels fed by gravity or lifted by a pump. A weir and sluice manage the flow, and the laterals are spaced to avoid either drowning or drought. It needs a mill system with leats (channels), levelling skill and good water rights. Poor drainage with irrigation leaves salt in the soil.

name: Terracing
note: Cutting hillsides into flat benches so crops can be grown on slopes without the soil washing away. The crucial detail is a slight inward slope of each bench, which keeps water on the bench instead of running off the outer edge. It needs stone walls, much labour and drainage. A failing wall lets the whole terrace slump.

name: Contour ploughing
note: Contour ploughing means ploughing along lines of equal height across a slope instead of straight up and down it. Each furrow then acts as a small barrier that slows rainwater, so more soaks in and less soil is washed away. It needs the contour lines marked out first with some levelling method, and the plough has to follow curved lines, which is slower and more awkward than straight furrows.

name: Erosion control - wind breaks and mulch
note: The spacing of shelterbelts for protection depth and the depth of mulch that protects soil without smothering germination

name: Record-keeping and breeding selection
note: Systematic selection of the best plants for breeding. The discipline needed is to isolate traits, to prevent cross-pollination from other varieties and to observe for many years. It needs written records and the habit of controlled experiments. It improves crops slowly but surely; without records, good plants are lost in the mix.

name: Controlled pollination
note: Hand-pollinate selected plants using brushes to cross desired traits: large seeds with disease resistance, for instance. Works on grains and legumes. Requires understanding flower anatomy and patience; gains compound with pedigree records.

name: Hybridisation
note: Crossing two different pure lines to produce offspring that are more vigorous than either parent. First, plants are inbred over generations until their vigour is nearly gone (inbreeding to extinction), then two such lines are crossed and vigour returns (heterosis). It needs controlled pollination. The seed must be bought fresh each year, because the hybrid's own seed does not breed true.

name: Hybrid maize
note: Maize grown from the cross of two inbred lines. The discovery was that yield rises across the board because hybrid plants show superior roots and kernels. It needs hybridisation and pure line selection. Farmers must buy fresh seed every year, since seed saved from a hybrid crop yields poorly.

name: Pure line selection
note: Selecting and inbreeding plants over generations to get a uniform line that breeds true. The counterintuitive insight is that inbreeding purifies traits so they pass on reliably, even as vigour drops. It needs record-keeping and breeding selection, and a garden. It is the first step to hybrid crops.

name: The seed trade
note: A trade in seed of known varieties. Isolation fields prevent cross-pollination, and testing plots verify purity before sale. It needs record-keeping and breeding selection, and merchants who can store and ship seed. Buyers must trust the seller, and mixed or old seed ruins a crop.

name: Seed certification
note: A system that tests and certifies seed before sale. The standard germination test shows how many seeds sprout, and the genetic purity test confirms it is the stated variety. It needs a seed trade and soil testing methods, and an inspector or body trusted to certify. It protects farmers from fraud.

name: Grafting
note: Joining a shoot (scion) from one tree to the rooted stock of another so the two grow as one. Success depends on the cambium (the thin growing layer under the bark) of both pieces touching, and on timing, usually in dormancy. Not every combination works: they must be close relatives. It needs a sharp knife, binding and wax. It copies a good variety exactly, which seed cannot do.

name: Budding
note: A form of grafting that uses a single bud, not a whole shoot. A bud is slipped under the bark of the rootstock at a time when the bark lifts easily, and it heals over during summer, and grows the following spring. It needs grafting skill, a sharp knife and good timing. It saves scion wood, and many buds can come from one shoot.

name: Layering
note: Making a new plant by bending a branch down so a part of it touches the soil, or wrapping a branch with moss, so that it grows roots while still attached to the parent. It takes one or two seasons for roots to form. Moisture must be maintained. It needs no tools. The new plant is a copy of the parent.

name: Rootstocks as knowledge
note: Rootstocks are the root systems onto which fruit trees are grafted. They differ in vigour, soil tolerance and the size of the tree they produce, so a grower can match a rootstock to the field conditions and the tree size wanted. It needs grafting and years of trial. A poorly matched rootstock can cause a weak or unproductive tree.

name: Plant quarantine
note: Holding imported plants in isolation before they are released, so that any diseases or pests show themselves before they spread. The isolation period allows disease symptoms to show, and inspectors check against criteria for known pests. It needs the principle of quarantine and controlled observation. Cutting corners can import a plague that ruins a whole crop.

name: Botanic garden as instrument of empire
note: A garden that collects, grows and studies plants from all over the world, used by empires to move valuable crops between colonies. Shipments were staggered, sent from several gardens, so that a crop could not be lost in a single voyage. It needs gardeners, ships and a network of correspondents. Plants die on long voyages unless they are protected.

name: The Wardian case
note: A sealed glass case in which plants carry their own moisture: water evaporates, condenses on the glass and drips back, making a small closed ecosystem. It keeps tropical cuttings alive for months at sea. It needs clear soda-lime glass and fine laboratory glassware skills. It lets the founder move plants across the world, which was nearly impossible before.

name: Sugar cultivation after voyage
note: Establishing sugar cane in a new land after carrying cuttings across the sea. Once a few cuttings take root, the plantation can be harvested continuously, with harvest planning and burn timing (cane is burned before cutting) to prevent disease. It needs eastern trade routes to bring the plants, a suitable warm climate and mills.

name: Tea cultivation after voyage
note: Establishing tea plantations in a new land after bringing plants. Tea requires high altitude, shade trees and careful timing of plucking; it takes years before the first harvest after planting. It needs a botanic garden to supply plants and a hill country with the right climate. Without the knowledge of how the leaf is processed, a plantation yields little.

name: Coffee cultivation after voyage
note: Establishing coffee in a new land after bringing seedlings or seed. Shade trees and altitude matching matter, and it takes years before the first harvest after planting. It needs eastern trade routes and a suitable climate. Seed loses its ability to sprout quickly, so it must be planted soon after the journey.

name: Potato from the New World
note: Bringing the potato from the Americas. One successful voyage is enough, because it propagates forever via tubers (the potatoes themselves are planted). Varieties diverge by latitude and day length: a variety from the tropics does not set tubers in long summer days. It needs a voyage across the Atlantic. Reliance on one variety invites disease.

name: Maize from the New World
note: Bringing maize from the Americas. Flint varieties (hard-kernelled) travelled farther north than dent varieties, and indigenous varieties for each region arose within decades from crossing and selection. It needs a voyage across the Atlantic. Maize needs warm summers and deep soil to ripen.

name: Bordeaux mixture
note: A fungicide made by mixing copper sulphate with lime in water and spraying it on vines and fruit trees to stop mildew. The precise ratio of copper to lime and the timing relative to rain prevent phytotoxicity (the spray burning the plant). It needs sulphuric acid (oil of vitriol), copper and slaked lime. Too much copper scorches leaves; too little protects nothing.

name: Lime sulphur
note: A spray made by boiling sulphur with lime in water, which makes a polysulphide solution that kills fungi and mites. The boiling time is what converts the sulphur into polysulphide, and the mixture must be stable on cold mornings. It needs sulphur, quicklime and sulphuric acid. It burns leaves in hot weather.

name: Lead arsenate
note: An insecticide made by combining a lead salt with arsenic. It is insoluble, so it clings to leaves without being washed off by rain. It needs lead and arsenic compounds. It is poisonous to people, and the concern about residue on harvested fruit and in the soil emerges late. Workers must use care when mixing and spraying it.

name: Nicotine as pesticide
note: An insecticide extracted from tobacco waste and turned into a sulphate salt to make it soluble in water. It is a neurotoxin that works on insects before mammals notice, but it is poisonous to people too. It needs tobacco waste and sulphuric acid. Aphids and soft-bodied insects are controlled, but spraying needs protective care.

name: Pyrethrum
unheld_reason: no sourced start civilisation used pyrethrum as an insecticide
note: An insecticide made from the dried flower heads of a daisy-like plant grown in highlands. The flowers are dried and ground or extracted, and the active compound kills insects on contact. It degrades rapidly in sunlight, so evening spraying matters. It needs pyrethrum planting stock and highland farmland. It is much less harmful to mammals than metal poisons.

name: DDT
note: A powerful synthetic insecticide, a chlorinated hydrocarbon made from chlorine, benzene and other chemicals. Persistence is the point and the peril: it stays active for a long time, but it accumulates in the fat of wildlife and thins the shells of birds' eggs, with effects decades later. It needs a chlor-alkali plant, benzene from coal tar and sulphuric acid.

name: The sprayer
note: A device with a pump that puts liquid pesticide under pressure and sends it through a nozzle as a fine spray. The nozzle geometry and pressure produce droplets fine enough to coat leaves without dripping waste. It needs a horse hoe for the crop rows, pumps and nozzles made to tolerance. Blocked nozzles give streaky coverage.

name: Biological control
note: The discipline of rearing and release timing, and the risk that introduced enemies become pests themselves

name: The resistant variety
note: The test crosses that confirm resistance is stable, and resistance-breaking mutant pests that emerge within years

name: Herd book
note: Progeny performance, not body scores, is what a herd book records to identify prepotent sires

name: Progeny testing
note: A bull can appear muscular but produce weak calves; progeny testing separates appearance from breeding value

name: Milking machine
note: The pulsation cycle that prevents sphincter closure, and rubber teat cups that don't lacerate

name: Cream separator
note: Bowl speed critical - too slow leaves cream in skim, too fast shatters fat globules into foam

name: Artificial insemination in cattle
note: Timing ovulation by oestrus observation and the catheter technique that reaches the cervix without trauma

name: Silage and the silo
note: Lactobacillus fermentation that produces lactic acid; pH drop halts spoilage at 3.8-4.0 in 3-6 weeks

hazard_counters.label: fodder that keeps through a bad winter

name: Balanced ration
note: The Wolff-Lehmann standard that calculates feed units by proximate analysis, not arbitrary eye assessment

name: Veterinary vaccination
note: Rinderpest vaccine and foot-and-mouth challenge - which diseases are vaccinated determines flock health risk

name: Cattle tuberculin test
note: Mantoux test: intradermal injection of purified protein derivative; delayed hypersensitivity reaction; induration size interpretation; active vs latent TB

name: Sheep dip
note: Temperature, immersion duration, and replenishment frequency that kill parasites without poisoning wool

name: Battery poultry
note: Birds never see soil or natural light; welfare costs are paid years later in disease epidemic risk

name: Roller milling
kb: Smooth metal cylinders crushing grain between them instead of grinding stones, producing finer flour faster.
note: Multiple roller pairs at increasing pressure produce granulated flour in a single pass without reheating

name: The purifier
note: Tapers in the air chamber that separate by density without leaving flour dust in the exhaust

name: White flour and vitamin loss
note: The discovery correlating white bread dominance with beriberi and pellagra epidemics in refined-grain populations

name: Yeast culture
note: Pure culture ferments faster, cleaner flavour, lower acetobacter infection rate, consistent results

name: Malting
note: Enzyme activation by moisture and temperature, then kiln-drying to halt germination at the right time

name: Mashing
note: Temperature holds and rests that allow amylase and protease to complete hydrolysis without denaturing

name: Hopping
unheld_reason: hopped beer reaches England after 1300; Norse hop growing is not attested
note: Alpha acid isomerisation by boil time, late additions for aroma - extraction curves that changed brewing

name: Fermentation control
note: Acetobacter infection control by nitrogen blanking and acid production, removing risk of vinegar accident

name: The hydrometer
note: The alcohol yield calculation from gravity drop and the fermentation stop point you can read precisely

name: Pot still distillation
note: Copper construction prevents sulphide buildup; distiller skill is in heads-hearts-tails cut timing

name: Column still
note: Rectifying columns that eliminate headache-causing congeners, producing neutral spirits from any fermented base

name: Cheese families
note: Hard cheeses start with cut curd cooked high, soft with whole milk curdled low - technique differences are vast

name: Butter
note: The inversion of emulsion where fat phase becomes continuous and buttermilk phase separates out

name: Condensed milk
note: Vacuum boiling at low temperature prevents caramelisation; sugar saturation prevents crystallisation

name: Evaporated milk
note: The homogenisation that prevents cream separation during long shelf life and the heat-shock that stabilises casein

name: Oil pressing
note: Cold press preserves flavour but hot press from preheated seeds extracts more oil at cost of quality

name: Fat hydrogenation
note: Temperature control to avoid polymerisation; partial hydrogenation creates trans-fats unknowingly

name: Cane and beet sugar refining
note: Multiple crystallisations from A, B, C molasses requiring skill in grain size and temperature management

name: Vacuum pan for sugar
note: Vacuum reduces boiling point; precise temperature and duration that makes small crystals without burning sugar

name: The centrifugal machine for sugar
note: Vibration that prevents sugar from caking against the screen and the automated discharge timer

name: Canning
note: Botulism toxin prevention by adequate temperature and time, plus the headspace air displacement

name: The retort
note: Temperature logging to confirm adequate heat penetration to the can centre, pressure gauge accuracy

name: Double seam can
note: The pressure-sealing geometry and tool wear that prevents leakage during handling and retort pressure

name: Bottling
note: Bottle standardisation and cork sealing that prevents oxidation and breakage

name: Crown cork
note: Crimped tin cap with cork liner, seals carbonated beverages, bottling machine applies caps, invented 1891

name: Pasteurisation
note: Heat milk to 63-65 C for 30 minutes or 72 C for 15 seconds, then cool rapidly. Kills spoilage bacteria and pathogens without destroying nutritional value or flavor of fresh milk. Works without germ theory; empirically known to prevent souring and spoilage.

name: Refrigeration - ice trade
note: Sawing, stacking with sawdust insulation, transport timing that prevents melt before delivery

name: Cold store
note: Insulation thickness, air circulation path, and humidity control that prevents condensation and drip

name: Refrigerated ship
note: Engine-driven compressor that maintains holds at -15C during weeks at sea; odour and cross-contamination problems

name: Nitrite curing
note: Nitrous acid formation and its bacteriostatic action; N-nitrosamine formation during storage is carcinogenic

name: Food laboratory and testing
note: Gravimetric fat and protein, acidimetry for pH, microscopy for moulds - methods that define food standards

name: Adulteration law and enforcement
note: The Pure Food Act that created food inspection; enforcement scale determines whether regulation reduces fraud
